nodes.title: Formal languages and deductive systems
nodes.description: Formal syntax specifies which symbol strings count as mathematical expressions. A proof system specifies permitted inferential steps.

nodes.title: Syntax
nodes.description: Formal syntax specifies which symbol strings count as mathematical expressions. Precise formation rules make proofs and substitutions objects that can themselves be studied.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Terms and formulas
nodes.description: Terms name objects, while formulas express relations and assertions about them. Inductive formation rules define both classes.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Free and bound variables
nodes.description: A variable occurrence is bound when governed by a quantifier and free otherwise. This distinction determines what a formula depends on.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Substitution
nodes.description: Substitution replaces free variables by terms while avoiding unintended variable capture. Its formal rules are needed for sound inference and coding arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Proof systems
nodes.description: A proof system specifies permitted inferential steps. Soundness connects those syntactic steps to semantic truth.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Natural deduction
nodes.description: Natural deduction uses introduction and elimination rules for logical connectives and quantifiers. It closely reflects ordinary structured proof reasoning.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Sequent calculus
nodes.description: Sequent calculus represents entailments with antecedent and consequent collections. Its rule structure is suited to structural and cut-elimination arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Soundness
nodes.description: Soundness means that derivable consequences are semantically valid in the intended class of structures. It is proved by checking the inference rules.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: First-order semantics
nodes.description: First-order semantics interprets formulas in mathematical structures. Completeness makes semantic consequence accessible through formal deduction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Structures and satisfaction
nodes.description: First-order semantics interprets formulas in mathematical structures. Satisfaction makes truth depend on the structure and any assignment to free variables.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Interpretations
nodes.description: An interpretation assigns a domain and meanings to relation, function, and constant symbols. This turns formal language into a mathematical structure.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Truth
nodes.description: Truth is defined recursively from atomic formulas through connectives and quantifiers. Sentences have truth values without free-variable assignments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Elementary equivalence
nodes.description: Elementarily equivalent structures satisfy the same first-order sentences. They can still differ in size or be nonisomorphic.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Completeness and compactness
nodes.description: Completeness makes semantic consequence accessible through formal deduction. Compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem expose its consequences for model construction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Completeness theorem
nodes.description: First-order completeness states that every semantic consequence has a formal proof in a sound complete calculus. It concerns consequence, not the completeness of every axiomatic theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Compactness theorem
nodes.description: Compactness says that a set of first-order sentences has a model if every finite subset does. It turns finite consistency checks into a global existence result.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Löwenheim–Skolem
nodes.description: Löwenheim–Skolem theorems control model sizes relative to language cardinality. They reveal limits on first-order characterization of infinite structures.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Model theory
nodes.description: Model theory studies theories through the structures satisfying them. Saturation and homogeneity concern realization of types and extension of partial symmetries.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Types and theories
nodes.description: Model theory studies theories through the structures satisfying them. Types describe possible configurations of elements within those structures.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Complete theories
nodes.description: A complete consistent theory decides every sentence in its language. This differs from a logic having a complete proof calculus.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Types
nodes.description: A type is a consistent collection of formulas describing a potential tuple over specified parameters. Realization of types measures how rich a model is.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Omitting types
nodes.description: Omitting-types theorems construct models that avoid selected nonprincipal types under countability hypotheses. They show that consistent descriptions need not occur in every model.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Saturated and homogeneous models
nodes.description: Saturation and homogeneity concern realization of types and extension of partial symmetries. They help construct and compare models systematically.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Elementary extensions
nodes.description: An elementary extension preserves truth of all formulas with parameters from the smaller structure. It enlarges the model without changing its first-order facts about existing elements.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Back-and-forth
nodes.description: Back-and-forth constructions extend compatible finite or small partial maps alternately in both directions. Under suitable hypotheses they produce isomorphisms.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Categoricity
nodes.description: Categoricity means uniqueness up to isomorphism among models of a specified cardinality. The cardinality and language setting are part of the claim.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Central Theory and Techniques
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Computability theory
nodes.description: Computability theory formalizes what an effective procedure can calculate. Undecidability identifies problems beyond any algorithm in the chosen model.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Turing computation
nodes.description: Computability theory formalizes what an effective procedure can calculate. Equivalent computational models make the notion robust.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Machines
nodes.description: A Turing machine performs local symbol operations according to finitely many rules. It provides a precise model of algorithmic computation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Recursive functions
nodes.description: Recursive-function formalisms define computable functions through basic functions and closure operations. Their equivalence with machine models links several views of effectiveness.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Universal programs
nodes.description: A universal program simulates other encoded programs. It enables self-reference and diagonal undecidability arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Undecidability
nodes.description: Undecidability identifies problems beyond any algorithm in the chosen model. Reductions organize these limitations into reusable comparisons.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Halting problem
nodes.description: The halting problem asks whether a coded program eventually stops on a coded input. No algorithm decides this for all program-input pairs.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Many-one reductions
nodes.description: A many-one reduction transforms instances computably while preserving yes-or-no membership. It transfers undecidability from one problem to another.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Recursively enumerable sets
nodes.description: A recursively enumerable set can have its members effectively listed or semidecided. Its complement need not be recursively enumerable.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Incompleteness and formal arithmetic
nodes.description: Formal arithmetic can represent basic computations and encode syntax numerically. Incompleteness limits effectively axiomatized theories strong enough to express arithmetic.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Representability
nodes.description: Formal arithmetic can represent basic computations and encode syntax numerically. These capabilities let a theory make statements about its own proofs.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Coding syntax
nodes.description: Gödel coding assigns natural numbers to expressions and finite proof sequences. It turns syntactic relations into arithmetic predicates.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Primitive recursive relations
nodes.description: Primitive recursive relations describe computations built by bounded structural recursion in the usual formalism. Their arithmetical representability supports proof coding.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Derivability conditions
nodes.description: Derivability conditions formalize how an internal provability predicate behaves. They are central hypotheses in standard proofs of the second incompleteness theorem.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Gödel theorems
nodes.description: Incompleteness limits effectively axiomatized theories strong enough to express arithmetic. The assumptions determine exactly which limitation follows.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: First and second incompleteness
nodes.description: The first theorem yields undecidable sentences for suitable consistent theories, and the second restricts internal proofs of their own consistency. Both concern sufficiently strong effective theories with appropriate formalizations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Consistency assumptions
nodes.description: Consistency and stronger soundness assumptions have distinct roles in different formulations. The selected theorem statement must say which assumption is actually used.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Scope
nodes.description: Incompleteness does not say that every mathematical statement is undecidable or that all theories are incomplete. Its scope is limited by effectiveness, strength, and consistency hypotheses.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Proof theory
nodes.description: Proof normalization removes redundant detours from formal deductions. Ordinal methods measure the complexity of proof reductions and induction principles.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Normalization and cut elimination
nodes.description: Proof normalization removes redundant detours from formal deductions. Cut elimination gives a related structural simplification in sequent systems.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Natural deduction normalization
nodes.description: Normalization transforms suitable natural-deduction proofs into normal forms without certain introduction-elimination detours. The result depends on the chosen logical system.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Sequent calculus
nodes.description: Sequent proofs display antecedents, conclusions, and structural rules explicitly. This organization makes proof transformations precise.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cut elimination
nodes.description: Cut elimination removes applications of a rule composing proofs through an intermediate formula in systems where the theorem holds. It yields structural consequences such as subformula properties in appropriate formulations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Ordinal methods
nodes.description: Ordinal methods measure the complexity of proof reductions and induction principles. They compare the strength of formal arithmetic systems.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Consistency proofs
nodes.description: A consistency proof rules out a derivation of contradiction relative to an ambient reasoning framework. Its assumptions must be stated when interpreting the conclusion.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Proof-theoretic ordinals
nodes.description: A proof-theoretic ordinal records an induction or well-ordering strength associated with a theory in a specified analysis. It is a calibrated invariant rather than an arbitrary rank.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Limits of formalization
nodes.description: Formal systems may be unable to internalize parts of their own metatheory. Incompleteness explains important limits on internal consistency arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Axiomatic set theory
nodes.description: Axiomatic set theory specifies the set-forming principles used as a mathematical foundation. Ordinals model well-ordered stages of iteration.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: ZF and ZFC
nodes.description: Axiomatic set theory specifies the set-forming principles used as a mathematical foundation. ZFC adds the axiom of choice to ZF.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Extensionality and foundation
nodes.description: Extensionality identifies sets with the same members, while foundation restricts membership descent. These axioms govern identity and the shape of the set universe.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Replacement
nodes.description: Replacement asserts that the image of a set under a definable functional relation is a set. It supports transfinite constructions beyond elementary separation.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Choice
nodes.description: Choice selects one element from each member of a family of nonempty sets. Its equivalent forms support many algebraic and topological existence arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Ordinals and recursion
nodes.description: Ordinals model well-ordered stages of iteration. Transfinite recursion extends ordinary recursive construction beyond finite indices.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Ordinal arithmetic
nodes.description: Ordinal arithmetic describes sums, products, and exponentiation of well-orders. It differs from cardinal arithmetic and is generally noncommutative.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Transfinite recursion
nodes.description: Transfinite recursion defines each stage using the already constructed earlier stages. It is fundamental to cumulative hierarchies and ordinal-indexed constructions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Well-orders
nodes.description: A well-order gives every nonempty subset a least element. This supports transfinite induction and identifies an order type represented by an ordinal.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cardinals and combinatorics
nodes.description: Cardinals compare sizes of sets independently of their ordering. Infinite combinatorics studies structured configurations within large sets and orders.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cardinal arithmetic
nodes.description: Cardinals compare sizes of sets independently of their ordering. Cofinality distinguishes different ways infinite sizes can be approached.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cardinal operations
nodes.description: Cardinal addition, multiplication, and exponentiation represent disjoint union, Cartesian product, and function sets. Their laws depend on whether choice is assumed.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Cofinality
nodes.description: Cofinality is the least size of an unbounded subset of an ordinal. It measures how many stages are needed to approach that ordinal.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Regular and singular cardinals
nodes.description: An infinite cardinal is regular when its cofinality equals itself and singular otherwise. This distinction strongly influences infinite combinatorics.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Combinatorial principles
nodes.description: Infinite combinatorics studies structured configurations within large sets and orders. Trees, stationary sets, and partition relations provide its basic languages.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Trees
nodes.description: A set-theoretic tree is a partially ordered set whose predecessor sets are well ordered. Branches and levels encode combinatorial possibilities and obstructions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Stationary sets
nodes.description: A stationary subset of a regular uncountable cardinal meets every closed unbounded subset. It captures a robust form of largeness beyond unboundedness.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Partition relations
nodes.description: Partition relations ask whether colorings admit large homogeneous subsets of prescribed type. They generalize finite Ramsey questions to infinite cardinals.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Further Theory and Applications
nodes.description: This part groups chapters in this subject’s graduate book.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Constructibility and independence
nodes.description: The constructible universe organizes sets by iterated definability. Independence means that an axiom system decides neither a statement nor its negation under stated consistency assumptions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Constructible universe
nodes.description: The constructible universe organizes sets by iterated definability. It is a canonical inner-model setting for relative-consistency arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: L and relative consistency
nodes.description: The universe L is built by taking definable subsets stage by stage along the ordinals. Its internal properties yield important relative-consistency results for choice and the continuum hypothesis.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Condensation overview
nodes.description: Condensation describes how suitable elementary pieces of levels of L collapse to other constructible levels. It reveals the hierarchy's fine structural regularity.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Independence results
nodes.description: Independence means that an axiom system decides neither a statement nor its negation under stated consistency assumptions. Inner models and forcing provide complementary directions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Continuum hypothesis
nodes.description: The continuum hypothesis fixes the size of the continuum relative to the first uncountable cardinal. Its independence from ZFC is interpreted through relative-consistency results.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Choice
nodes.description: The axiom of choice is independent of ZF in the standard relative-consistency sense. Models with and without choice illustrate its separate foundational role.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Interpretation of relative consistency
nodes.description: A relative-consistency statement says that consistency of one theory implies consistency of another. It does not establish absolute consistency of either theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Forcing and advanced foundations
nodes.description: Forcing constructs extensions of suitable ground models using partially ordered approximations. Advanced foundations compare model-building methods with alternative formal languages.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Forcing basics
nodes.description: Forcing constructs extensions of suitable ground models using partially ordered approximations. Names and generic filters define the objects appearing in those extensions.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Partial orders
nodes.description: Forcing conditions represent partial information ordered by strength. The partial order determines what the extension is designed to add or preserve.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Names
nodes.description: Forcing names are recursively built instructions for objects in the extension. A generic filter interprets those instructions as actual sets.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Generic extensions
nodes.description: A generic filter meets the dense sets required by the chosen ground-model setup. Its extension satisfies the forcing theorem and preserves specified axioms under the standard construction.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Applications and alternatives
nodes.description: Advanced foundations compare model-building methods with alternative formal languages. The final route should keep mathematical results distinct from philosophical interpretations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Independence proofs
nodes.description: An independence proof constructs or interprets models with opposing truth values for a statement. It must record the background consistency assumptions and preservation arguments.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Type theory
nodes.description: Type theory organizes expressions by types and formation rules rather than a single unrestricted membership relation. Different type theories offer different logical and computational foundations.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.

nodes.title: Constructive or categorical foundations
nodes.description: Constructive and categorical foundations emphasize proof content or structural relationships in different ways. Their exact axioms must be specified before comparing their strength with set theory.
nodes.evidence: Book organization only; this arrow layer makes no proof-dependency claim.
